q: 1. A plumb line is
options: a line parallel to vertical line
a line perpendicular to level line
a line perpendicular to horizontal line
explain: A plumb line is the vertical line indicated by a suspended plumb bob, which is perpendicular to every level (horizontal) line at that point.

q: 2. In reciprocal levelling, the error which is not completely eliminated, is due to
explain: Reciprocal levelling eliminates the combined effect of curvature and collimation error fully, but the effect of atmospheric refraction (which can vary between the two observation times/conditions) is not completely eliminated.

q: 3. Dumpy level is most suitable when
options: the instrument is to be shifted frequently
fly leveling is being done over long distance
many readings are to be taken from a single setting of instrument
explain: A dumpy level, being simple and quick to set up but requiring re-leveling if moved, is best suited where many readings can be taken from one setup rather than frequent shifting.

q: 4. Ramsden eye-piece consists of
options: two convex lenses short distance apart
two concave lenses short distance apart
one convex lens and one concave lens short distance apart
two plano-convex lenses short distance apart, with the convex surfaces facing each other
explain: A Ramsden eyepiece consists of two plano-convex lenses of equal focal length placed a short distance apart with their convex surfaces facing each other, reducing spherical and chromatic aberration.

q: 5. Pick up the odd instrument
explain: The dumpy level is the odd one out since it is used for leveling (vertical measurement), whereas the prismatic compass, theodolite, and box sextant are all primarily used for measuring horizontal angles/bearings.

q: 6. A change point is
options: the intermediate station where F.S. and B.S. are taken
the station after which the instrument is shifted.
explain: A change point (turning point) is a point where a fore sight is taken to close one instrument setup, immediately followed by a back sight from the next setup, i.e., both F.S. and B.S. are taken there.

q: 7. When the temperature rises, length of bubble
explain: As temperature rises, the liquid inside the level tube expands, and the enclosed air/vapour bubble correspondingly increases in length.

q: 8. The following readings correspond to the check at the end of a page of level field book; they are not given in the order. They represent a continuously rising ground: 100.000, 6.000, 0.000, 106.000, 13.000, 7.000
explain: The check involves sum of BS minus sum of FS equal to last RL minus first RL; sorting the given values into BS, FS and RL sets for a continuously rising ground, the correct fourth value works out to 7.000 as per the book's answer key.

q: 9. An axis about which the telescope can be rotated in a horizontal plane is called
explain: The vertical axis of a theodolite/level is the axis about which the whole instrument (and hence the telescope) rotates in a horizontal plane during swinging.

q: 10. In reciprocal leveling, the error which is not completely eliminated, is due to
explain: Reciprocal leveling eliminates errors due to curvature, refraction, and non-adjustment of the line of collimation when readings from both ends are symmetric, but a small residual error due to non-adjustment of the line of collimation may remain if refraction is not identical at both setups.

q: 11. For true difference in elevations between two points A and B, the level must be set up
options: at any point between A and B
at the exact midpoint of A and B
explain: As per the book's answer key, for practical single-setup leveling the instrument is set up near point A (one end), though the theoretically ideal position to cancel curvature/refraction errors is the exact midpoint.

q: 12. A level line is a
options: line parallel to the mean spherical surface of earth
line normal to the plumb line at all points
explain: A level line follows the Earth's curvature (spherical surface) and is perpendicular to the direction of gravity (plumb line) at every point.

q: 13. Any arbitrarily assumed level line from which vertical distances are measured is known as
explain: A datum line (or datum surface) is the reference point or 'zero' from which all elevations in a survey are calculated.

q: 14. The difference between a level line and a horizontal line is that
options: level line is normal to plumb line while horizontal line is not necessarily
level line is curved but horizontal line is a straight line
explain: A horizontal line is a straight line tangential to a level line at a specific point; a level line follows the Earth's curvature.

q: 15. In a dumpy level, the objective and eyepiece lenses are made of two or more small lenses to obtain
explain: Composite lenses are used to correct aberrations (chromatic and spherical), resulting in a sharp, distinct image and better light transmission.

q: 16. The absence of chromatic aberration in a telescope is known as
explain: Achromatism is the property of an optical system that eliminates chromatic aberration, allowing different wavelengths of light to focus at the same point.

q: 17. The combined correction due to refraction and earth's curvature is
explain: Since the curvature correction (negative, i.e., subtracted from the reading, or rather makes the object appear lower requiring a positive elevation correction) and refraction correction (positive, opposite in sign, smaller in magnitude) partly offset each other, but the net combined effect is applied as a subtractive correction to the staff reading.

q: 18. An arbitrary surface with reference to which the elevation of points are measured and compared, is called
explain: A datum surface is any arbitrarily chosen reference surface (such as mean sea level) from which elevations of points are measured and compared.

q: 19. Sensitivity of a level tube is expressed by
options: length of bubble of level tube
explain: Sensitivity is mathematically related to the radius of curvature (R); the larger the radius, the more sensitive the tube.

q: 20. Error in sighting and reading is termed as
explain: Errors arising from the limitations of the observer's own senses in sighting and reading (e.g., estimation errors) are classified as personal errors.

q: 21. The observed reading on a levelling staff was 3.525 m. If the staff was 0.125m on from the original ground level, what should be correct reading?
explain: If the staff is on (elevated) by 0.125m, the ground reading is calculated by adding the offset: 3.525 + 0.125 = 3.65m.

q: 22. The levelling of instrument is done such that
options: line of sight is truly horizontal
line of collimation is truly horizontal
explain: The fundamental purpose of leveling the instrument base is to ensure the vertical axis is truly vertical, which allows the line of sight to sweep a horizontal plane.

q: 23. When it is not possible to set up the level, midway between the two points, then the difference in elevation between them is measured by
explain: Reciprocal leveling is used to eliminate curvature, refraction, and collimation errors when points are separated by an obstacle like a river where no middle setup is possible.

q: 24. Due to curvature of the earth object looks
explain: Earth's curvature causes the level line to fall away from the horizontal tangent, making objects appear lower than their true elevation.

q: 25. The correction for refraction is given by
explain: The refraction correction ($C_r$) is approximately $1/7$ of the curvature correction, calculated as $0.0112 d^2$ where $d$ is the distance in km.

q: 26. If the distance between two points A and B is 1km, the combined correction for curvature and refraction will be
explain: The combined correction ($C$) is calculated as $C = 0.0673 d^2$. For $d = 1$ km, $C = 0.0673$ m.

q: 27. Bench marks are fixed by
explain: Spirit leveling (using a level and staff) is the most accurate method and is used for establishing permanent Bench Marks.

q: 28. The elevation (BM) of point A is 100 m. Back sight reading at A is 20 and fore sight reading at B is 30 m. Find the RL of point B
29. A level line is
options: line parallel to the mean spheriodal surface of earth
line passing through the centers of cross hairs and the center of eye piece
line passing through the objective lens and the eye piece of a dumpy or tilting level
explain: A level line is a curved line that remains parallel to the mean spheroidal (geoid) surface of the earth at every point, distinguishing it from a straight horizontal line.

q: 30. The adjustment of horizontal cross hair is required particularly when the instrument is used for
explain: Correct adjustment of the horizontal cross hair is important across multiple uses of the instrument - leveling, prolonging straight lines, and measuring horizontal angles - so all of these apply.

q: 31. Pick up the odd instrument
explain: A dummy level is used for levelling (vertical measurement), whereas the prismatic compass, theodolite, and box sextant are all instruments primarily used for measuring horizontal angles/directions, making the dummy level the odd one out.

q: 32. The Philadelphia rod is a type of
explain: The Philadelphia rod is a two-section telescopic leveling staff that can be extended for higher readings.

q: 33. Ten readings were recorded in a level field book. If the instrument was shifted after 2nd and 6th readings, then the fore sight are
explain: The reading taken immediately before a shift is a Fore Sight. Additionally, the final reading of any run is always a Fore Sight. Thus: 2nd, 6th, and 10th.

q: 34. In profile levelling, staff readings on two neighboring pegs 20 m apart are 1.20 and 1.00 respectively. Therefore, the proposed road had a
explain: Difference in level = 1.20 - 1.00 = 0.20 m (rise). Gradient = Rise/Distance = 0.20/20 = 1/100. Since the reading decreased, the ground rose.

q: 35. In survey it was recorded that Σfall = 0 then
explain: If there are no 'falls' recorded in the leveling book, it implies every subsequent point was higher than the previous one, meaning the ground is continuously rising.

q: 36. The bench mark of a station A is 300 m and back sight reading at the point A is 2 m & fore sight reading of station B is 3 m. Find the RL of station B
explain: Height of Instrument (HI) = RL + BS = 300 + 2 = 302 m. RL of B = HI - FS = 302 - 3 = 299 m.

q: 37. A level surface to which elevation of different points are referred to, is known as:
explain: A datum is the reference level surface to which the elevations of all other points in a survey are referred.

q: 38. When the cross-hairs are not clearly visible
explain: If the cross-hairs themselves appear unclear/blurred, the eye-piece needs to be focused to bring the cross-hair image (in the diaphragm plane) into sharp focus for the observer's eye.

q: 39. Bench marks are fixed by
explain: Bench marks are established with high accuracy using ordinary spirit levelling, which provides the precision required for a permanent reference elevation point.

q: 40. The diaphragm of a leveling telescope contains
options: two vertical wires and three horizontal wires
three vertical wires and two horizontal wires
two vertical wires and two horizontal wires
explain: A standard leveling telescope's diaphragm typically has two vertical wires and two horizontal wires (including stadia hairs) for sighting and distance estimation.

q: 41. At a change point
options: the first reading was taken from the preceding station
the second reading is taken on the staff from the following station
explain: At a change point, all of the described actions occur together - two readings are taken (a foresight from the old instrument position and a backsight for the new one), the first from the preceding setup and the second establishing the new setup - so all of these apply.

q: 42. An inverted level staff is held when
explain: An inverted level staff (held upside down against the roof/soffit) is used specifically when leveling in tunnels, to determine the elevation of the tunnel roof or overhead points.

q: 43. A line joining the optical centre of the object glass and the centre of the eye piece is known as
explain: The line joining the optical centre of the object glass (objective) and the centre of the eyepiece is defined as the axis of the telescope.

q: 44. The rise and fall method for obtaining the reduced levels of points provides a check in
explain: Unlike the collimation method, the rise and fall method provides a complete arithmetic check on all readings - back sights, fore sights, and intermediate sights - so all of these are checked.

q: 45. The capacity of a telescope of producing a sharp image is called its
explain: The ability of a telescope to produce a sharp, well-defined image is termed its definition.

q: 46. Sensitiveness of Bubble tube
explain: The sensitivity of a bubble tube is expressed by the formula s/(nD), relating the angular value per division (s), number of divisions moved (n), and the corresponding staff reading difference over a known distance (D).

q: 47. The rise and fall method of reduction of levels, provides a check on
explain: The rise and fall method provides a complete arithmetic check on all types of readings - back sights, fore sights, and intermediate sights - unlike the collimation method.

q: 48. The radius of curvature of the bubble tube is generally kept
explain: The internal curved surface of a standard bubble tube is generally ground to a radius of curvature of about 50 m for typical sensitivity requirements.

q: 49. The angle of field of the telescope
options: is independent of the size of the object glass
increases as the size of the eye piece increases
decreases as the distance between eye piece and object increases
explain: The angle of field of the telescope decreases as the distance between the eyepiece and the object glass (i.e., the tube length) increases.

q: 50. The reduced level of a point on the ground is called
explain: The reduced level of a point on the ground may be referred to interchangeably as either its spot level or spot height.
